/Issued 235 PM MDT Thu Sep 24 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

Ridging aloft will begin to break down late Friday, but not 
before unseasonably warm and dry conditions persist for another 
day. A potent negatively tilted Pacific trough and attendant cold 
front are poised to move through the Northern Rockies late Friday 
afternoon through early Saturday. H500/H700 south/southwesterly 
flow increases to the 30 to 50 kt range by Friday afternoon, with 
some of this reaching the surface amid deep layer mixing. Surface 
winds will be strongest and most impactful over the high plains 
along the Rocky Mountain Front during the cold frontal passage 
Friday evening. While it will be breezy to windy for 
central/north-central locations to the east, there will be a 
shorter opportunity for wind gusts exceeding 50 mph and higher 
dependency on isolated shower and thunderstorm activity 
transferring the stronger flow aloft to the surface.

There will be little precipitation of consequence with this 
system; however, H700 temperatures quickly falling to around -5C 
Friday night will initiate a period of light accumulating snow 
over the higher terrain (above 6000 ft) of Glacier National Park, 
including the Logan Pass area by Saturday morning. More seasonable
temperatures will filter in behind the front on Saturday, with 
gusty westerly winds lingering over the plains through the early 
afternoon hours.

Another Pacific trough looks to move through Sunday into Monday. 
This one will be weaker with the core of the system's energy 
staying well south of the forecast area. The primary change to the
sensible weather will be increased shower activity for 
southwestern Montana and continued areawide seasonably cool 
temperatures. Then a broad trough will bring increased westerly 
flow for breezy to windy conditions heading towards the mid-week 
period of next week. - RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Gusty to Strong Winds Late Friday into Saturday...

The primary concern continues to be strong winds associated with 
Pacific cold front Friday evening through early Saturday. South to
southwesterly winds begin increasing in advance of the front 
Friday afternoon with gusts mostly in the 25 to 35 mph range. The 
combination of gusty winds with the unseasonably warm conditions 
will bring localized fire weather concerns, although lingering 
ground moisture will preclude widespread elevated fire conditions.


The cold front looks to cross the Continental Divide roughly 
between 5 and 10 pm MDT. Strong westerly winds will be most 
widespread and persistent over the high plains along the Rocky 
Mountain Front due to the cold frontal passage in the evening and 
then mountain wave activity overnight. There is over a 70% chance 
for wind gusts exceeding 55 mph and over a 50% chance for 
sustained winds exceeding 40 mph. Reasonable high end wind gusts 
(90th percentile) will be around 70 mph, particularly for areas 
along and west of highway 89 from Chouteau to US highway 2 and 
then for areas west of I15 north of the Highline. With this in 
mind, the high wind watch was expanded to include the Southern 
Rocky Mountain Front Plains zone. Technically high wind criteria 
is 75 mph for gusts and 50 mph for sustained winds for both Rocky 
Mountain Front Plains zones, but the high wind watch seems 
warranted given this is the first high wind event of the fall 
season, trees being mostly fully leafed, and the amount of 
lingering summer recreation traffic. 

The stronger winds for central and north-central areas east of 
I15 will be less consistent and more dependent on the dynamics of 
the front and isolated convection to transfer the stronger flow to
the surface. Moreover, the temporal window of opportunity will 
generally be less than three hours. Given these factors, I have 
elected to hold off on high wind products for now. 

There was some consideration given to extend the high wind 
watches through Saturday afternoon with diurnal mixing looking to 
bring another round of gusty winds; however, the upper level flow 
weakens substantially and ultimately looks to diminishes the 
occurrence of widespread criteria winds. 

Glacier National Park Light Accumulating Snow Saturday Morning...

There will be strong cold air advection behind this front with 
snow levels crashing to as low as 5000 ft along the Rocky Mountain
Front. The 90th percentile of snowfall of 1 to 3 inches seems 
reasonable for areas of Glacier National Park above 6000 ft given 
the synoptic setup. Impacts will be most felt for those recreating
in the park or for those responsible for maintenance late Friday 
night and Saturday morning. - RCG
